prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated without trap-induced shifts, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B007 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. After the first round the case rests on three points that all eight files accept. First, the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct physical idea: choose the trap wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, and many neutral atoms can be held and interrogated without perturbation. That is what turns the statistics of an atom ensemble into a stability advantage. Second, the result is reproduced. JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL report agreeing uncertainties near 1e-18, and clock-to-clock comparisons, including over fibre, close the loop. In my own field a claim of that kind is only believed when independent systematic budgets agree, and here they do. Third, the use is concrete: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, and the basis of the redefinition of the second. For the citation I now propose wording that names the mechanism (neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, many atoms interrogated at once) and not the generic term 'optical clock'. That answers the chair's question about how to separate this from the 2005 comb prize (counting optical cycles) and the 2012 ion-control prize (single trapped quantum systems), and it keeps the Al+ and Sr+ ion clocks, which reach comparable accuracy by a different route, outside the claim. Credit is Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice realisation, Ye for taking the system to extreme coherence, accuracy and many-body systematics.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is still the strongest objection, and I do not think it can be argued away completely. Mehlig is right that the magic-wavelength idea is engineering of a light shift and not the exposure of a new general mechanism, and Danielsson is right that the tests of constants and dark matter are mostly prospective, so the clock is an instrument whose discovery content lies ahead. I accept that reading as legitimate; I weigh it less than the measured seven-to-eight-order improvement and the independent verification. The second reservation is attribution at the edges: Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov and the ion-clock groups are outside the credited pair, and I am working from memory of the 2001-2003 record (Katori's proposal with Pal'chikov and Ovsiannikov, the early Sr lattice spectroscopy, then the JILA accuracy results from 2008 onward). That memory is not a substitute for a check against the primary papers, and I would ask for that check before the citation is final. Third, a two-name prize leaves out the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups that produced independent verifications, which are experiments I value highly.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B012 first as a discovery of something nature supplied, says support is thin and attribution is the weak point, and says my suggestion to wait for the redefinition of the second is a fair instinct because the discovery content of the clocks will be clearer afterwards.
responses.response: I have changed my mind on waiting, and his own argument is part of the reason. The clock record is already a measurement result with independent confirmation; the redefinition is an administrative step by the metrology bodies and will follow the performance, not create it. Waiting would make our timing depend on a process outside physics. On the substance I agree that the constants and dark-matter tests are still limits and not detections, so I would phrase the citation around the demonstrated accuracy and the method and not around those prospects. On IceCube, I cannot judge the AMANDA and DUMAND priority well, and his own view that Yoshida should be left out shows how unsettled the credit is. If a two-part prize were wanted, B012 with Halzen and Karle would need three seats, which cannot be combined with Katori and Ye within the limit of three persons, so as I see it B012 is a one-year-or-the-other alternative to B007, not a companion. I keep it as my second alternative because I accept that it is the strongest discovery case for those who weigh nature's clue above the instrument.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B007 with a citation based on the magic-wavelength principle, and notes the lattice clock, unlike the comb and the ion clock, allows a very large ensemble to be interrogated without perturbation, and that the science is settled whether or not the CGPM acts.
responses.response: I agree and accept her correction of my round-1 hesitation about waiting. I also take up her formulation for the citation, since it is the most precise answer to the chair's first question: the novelty is the cancellation of the trap light shift for a large ensemble, which is a different principle from counting cycles with a comb or from controlling single ions. Where I would add a measurement point is that the ensemble is a resource only because Ye's group and others controlled collisional and tunnelling shifts in the lattice; that is the part of the story the citation should not lose, and it is why Ye's credit is more than record accuracy. As the two members of the committee working closest to atomic physics, she and I should both check the 2001-2003 record, and I would welcome her reading of the primary papers on that point. I remain somewhat more sceptical than she is of B041 as a companion part: Hubbard simulation lacks a decisive many-body result that classical computation cannot reach.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B032 first, calls B007 a safe and deserving prize but says magic-wavelength trapping engineers a light shift and does not expose a new general mechanism, and says safety does not make it the strongest case. He also names B007 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I accept the distinction he draws, and it is partly right: this is an invention that enables a measurement, not a new law. But the Statutes list inventions as well as discoveries, and a technique that improves a measurement by orders of magnitude and is then used to look at nature differently (gravitational redshift over a millimetre, new bounds on constants) meets that standard in my view. On B032 I want to retract nothing from round 1 but make my point sharper. I do not doubt the physics of the fluctuation theorems. My difficulty is that the shortlist credit of four names is a problem he himself concedes cannot be reduced to three, and I cannot see which experiment I would cite as decisive, since the pulling and single-electron tests confirm an exact identity. If outside experts could settle priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert, I would reconsider it for a later year, but I would not put it ahead of B007 this year.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B044 to B007 after reflecting that his first ranking mixed field loyalty with the discovery criterion, disagrees with waiting for the SI redefinition, and says Katori and Ye do not need a third name.
responses.response: I appreciate that he applied that discipline to his own ranking, and I note that it is also why I keep B044 out of my own preferred configuration. My conflict disclosure on circuit QED stands: we both sit in the WACQT leadership, and I would not take part in a vote on B044 as an impartial member. On the third name I agree with him that the two-name credit is defensible, since adding, for instance, Lemonde or Derevianko would blur the concept-and-realisation logic of the citation, though I would still record in the minutes that the early priority needs an external check. On waiting for the redefinition, I now agree with him and have changed my view from round 1.

responses.point: Olsson supports B007, does not wait for the redefinition, and insists that the 2001-2003 proposal and the first lattice-clock papers be checked against the record before the citation is finalised, noting that Katori's and Ye's groups claim the first demonstration and the record accuracy differently.
responses.response: I agree that the check is the main unfinished item and that she is right to separate the first demonstration from the accuracy frontier. From memory, the proposal that fixes the concept is Katori's work with Pal'chikov and Ovsiannikov from 2001 to 2003, the first strontium lattice spectroscopy followed from Katori's group around 2003 to 2005, and the JILA systematics and accuracy results followed from 2008 onward. That is a recollection and not verified. If the check showed that Lemonde and Derevianko had a priority claim on the concept itself, I would want the citation reworded around 'development' with the two names and not around 'invention'; I would still not add a third name, since the credit would then change in character. Her disclosed connection to Tokyo does not seem to me a reason for her to recuse, but I would note it, and I would ask the chair to include it in the record.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from B012 to B007, adds that ion clocks (Al+, Sr+) reach comparable accuracy so the citation should name the lattice technique, and keeps B012 as an alternative if the committee wants a discovery about nature.
responses.response: I agree with his point on the ion clocks and have built it into the citation: it names neutral atoms at a magic wavelength explicitly. This is also my answer to his worry about continuation of 2005. The comb is the ruler, the ion clock is a different platform, and the lattice clock is a different way to reach the same performance with a large ensemble, so the prize does not repeat either of them. I note that his position on B012 is a position about discovery versus instrument, and I would like it to be stated plainly in the vote, not by a ballot alternative alone. I do not think it should be treated as a second prize part this year because of the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge yes but not by a wide margin.

The 2001-2003 priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice demonstrations, which I know from memory and which an external expert check should confirm before the citation is final.
Whether the credit for Katori and Ye alone is seen as fair to Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov and the independent verification groups at NIST, PTB and SYRTE.
Whether the committee will take a one-part prize; I see no second achievement that fits within the three-person limit alongside Katori and Ye with a settled interpretation.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B007: I have not collaborated with Katori or Ye. My PhD advisor was Svanberg and I spent a year in John Hall's lab during my PhD, which places me in the same broad precision-spectroscopy tradition as the clock community, but I have no joint work with the credited pair. For B044 (circuit QED) I repeat my disclosure that I sit on the executive management team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology with Johansson, and I would recuse myself if it became a serious option. I also note that I am on the management team of Deep Light Vision AB, which has no connection to any shortlisted achievement, and that I am listed as emeritus at Lund.
